chunks.text: Saribus rotundifolius, universally known by its common name 'footstool palm' and for decades classified under the genus name Livistona (as Livistona rotundifolia, still the name most plant nurseries and garden references use), is a solitary-trunked, evergreen fan palm reaching 15-25 m in typical accounts (with the article separately mentioning figures as low as 18 m and as high as 27 m, and exceptional individuals reportedly up to 45 m, so published height figures for this species vary considerably and should be treated as approximate). Its smooth, straight trunk, ringed with shallow old leaf-scar marks, carries spirally arranged, long-stalked, almost circular (hence 'rotundifolius', round-leaved) fan-shaped leaves roughly 1.2 m long, divided about halfway to the base into segments; young trees display a notably fresh green crown, and unlike many fan palms mature specimens rarely keep an untidy skirt of dead drooping leaves. Clusters of small three-petalled flowers develop into fleshy, roughly 2 cm fruit that ripen from brick-red through to black, and the tree flowers only once it is quite old, with bees reported as its pollinators; its foliage also hosts the caterpillars of at least two butterfly species, Suastus gremius and Elymnias hypermnestra. It is native to a fairly wide swath of island Southeast Asia — Sulawesi, the Maluku Islands and especially the Philippines, where it reaches its northernmost natural limit and is genuinely abundant, enough that its foliage is treated as the unofficial national leaf of the Philippines, known there as anáhaw. It has been introduced into cultivation (and in some cases naturalised into the wild, as happened on Java by the 1960s) across Peninsular Malaysia, Singapore, the Lesser Sunda Islands, Trinidad and Tobago, and India, and is widely planted as a landscaping and street palm. Practically, its large round leaves are put to direct use for thatching roofs and for wrapping food, though the article notes that repeated commercial leaf-harvesting measurably reduces subsequent leaf size, even though the palm regrows new leaves faster after cutting — a real sustainability trade-off for communities relying on it for thatch. Taxonomically, Jean-Baptiste Lamarck first described it in 1786 as Corypha rotundifolia; Carl Ludwig Blume proposed moving it to a new genus, Saribus (a name borrowed from a Maluku/Dutch colonial-era local name, sariboe), in the late 1830s, but this was not widely accepted and the species spent most of the 20th century filed under Livistona — it was only in 2011, on the strength of DNA-based phylogenetic research by Bacon and Baker, that Saribus was formally resurrected and the species moved back into it, which is why 'Livistona rotundifolia' remains the name most commonly encountered in older references and in the horticultural trade even today.

chunks.source: NParks Singapore FloraFaunaWeb — Livistona rotundifolia / Saribus rotundifolius
chunks.text: Singapore's National Parks Board flora database — which still primarily catalogues the species under the long-familiar name Livistona rotundifolia, reflecting how slowly the 2011 generic reclassification to Saribus has been adopted outside specialist botanical circles — records a maximum reported height toward the upper end of the range cited elsewhere, around 18-27 m, and confirms its standard practical uses of leaf thatching for roofing and leaf-wrapping for food, consistent with accounts from across its native and introduced range in Southeast Asia. As a widely grown landscape and streetscape palm across tropical Southeast Asian cities, it is valued for its neat, round-crowned silhouette and relatively slow, well-behaved single-trunk growth habit compared with faster-spreading or messier palm species, making it a popular 'tidy' ornamental choice for parks, institutional grounds and avenue plantings.
